claims.evidence: This is supported by growth data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claims.claim: Amygdalin degradation was confirmed for Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 and Bombilactobacillus strains BI-1.1 and BI-2.5.
claims.source: Using LC-MS analyses, amygdalin degradation was confirmed for strains that could grow in the presence of amygdalin as the sole carbon source, such as Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 (Figure 1H) and Bombilactobacillus strains BI-1.1 and BI-2.5 (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1H-I.

claims.claim: Bombilactobacillus strain BI-2.5 degrades less amygdalin when glucose is also present in the medium.
claims.source: Interestingly, Bombilactobacillus strain BI-2.5 degrades less amygdalin when glucose is also present in the medium (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1I.

claims.claim: For Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 and Bombilactobacillus strain BI-1.1, similar levels of amygdalin degradation were detected in cultures with or without glucose.
claims.source: For Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 and Bombilactobacillus strain BI-1.1, on the other hand, similar levels of amygdalin degradation were detected in cultures with or without glucose (Figure 1H–I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1H-I.

claims.claim: Amygdalin degradation was observed only for Gilliamella strain wkB112.
claims.source: We observed amygdalin degradation only for Gilliamella strain wkB112 (Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Metabolism of amygdalin by Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 and Bombilactobacillus strain BI-1.1 produces prunasin as a byproduct.
claims.source: Metabolism of amygdalin by Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 and Bombilactobacillus strain BI-1.1 produces prunasin as a byproduct (Figure 1L–M and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–H), although prunasin was only detected in wkB204 cultures after providing an excessive amount of amygdalin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1L-M and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-H.

claims.claim: Prunasin was not produced by Bombilactobacillus strain BI-2.5 or Gilliamella strain wkB112.
claims.source: On the other hand, prunasin was not produced by Bombilactobacillus strain BI-2.5 or Gilliamella strain wkB112 (Figure 1M–N) even after adding excess amygdalin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H–I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1M-N and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H-I.

claims.claim: Bombilactobacillus strain BI-2.5 and Gilliamella strain wkB112 metabolize amygdalin by breaking down the glycosidic bond that links the two glucose residues to the aglycone, releasing a disaccharide and mandelonitrile into the medium.
claims.source: Therefore, BI-2.5 and wkB112 seem to metabolize amygdalin in a different way than wkB204 and BI-1.1, probably by breaking down the glycosidic bond that links the two glucose residues to the aglycone, releasing a disaccharide and mandelonitrile into the medium.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these strains do not produce prunasin as an intermediate.

claims.claim: Amygdalin breakdown via a prunasin intermediate is limited to Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 and Bombilactobacillus strain BI-1.1.
claims.source: These results suggest that amygdalin breakdown via a prunasin intermediate is limited to wkB204 and BI-1.1.
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data showing prunasin production only in these strains (Figure 2).

claims.claim: The enzyme involved in amygdalin degradation by Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 is secreted.
claims.source: After finding that specific strains from different bee gut bacterial species can degrade amygdalin, we focused on honey bee-associated Bifidobacterium strains to investigate the enzyme involved in this metabolism. First, we checked whether the enzyme is secreted or not.
claims.evidence: This is supported by biochemical assays showing amygdalin degradation in spent medium (Figure 3B).

claims.claim: Spent medium of wkB204 amygdalin-grown cultures achieved full degradation of amygdalin.
claims.source: Since spent medium of wkB204 amygdalin-grown cultures achieved full degradation of amygdalin, we decided to characterize the secreted enzyme involved in the degradation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by biochemical assays shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Amygdalin-grown cultures of Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 had a distinct secretome when compared to glucose-grown cultures.
claims.source: Protein profiles were first obtained by SDS-PAGE gel and showed that amygdalin-grown cultures had a distinct secretome when compared to glucose-grown cultures (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE gel data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: 107 proteins were secreted in higher abundance in amygdalin-grown cultures of Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 compared to glucose-grown cultures.
claims.source: Then, samples were submitted to proteomics analysis, which confirmed the expression differences, as we found 107 proteins secreted in higher abundance in amygdalin-grown cultures and 131 proteins secreted in higher abundance in glucose-grown cultures (p<0.05, t-test followed by Benjamini-Hochberg procedure to control for false discovery, Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: 131 proteins were secreted in higher abundance in glucose-grown cultures of Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 compared to amygdalin-grown cultures.
claims.source: Then, samples were submitted to proteomics analysis, which confirmed the expression differences, as we found 107 proteins secreted in higher abundance in amygdalin-grown cultures and 131 proteins secreted in higher abundance in glucose-grown cultures (p<0.05, t-test followed by Benjamini-Hochberg procedure to control for false discovery, Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Several significantly upregulated proteins in amygdalin-grown cultures of Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 are associated with carbohydrate metabolism.
claims.source: Several significantly upregulated proteins in amygdalin-grown cultures are associated with carbohydrate metabolism (Figure 4—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4—source data 2.

claims.claim: A highly expressed enzyme belonging to the glycoside hydrolase family 3 (GH3) (WP_254476944) was detected only in amygdalin-grown cultures of Bifidobacterium strain wkB204.
claims.source: Interestingly, we detected a highly expressed enzyme belonging to the glycoside hydrolase family 3 (GH3) (WP_254476944) only in amygdalin-grown cultures (Figure 4C), suggesting its involvement in the observed degradation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Specific bacterial or fungal GH3 enzymes can degrade amygdalin.
claims.source: Other studies have demonstrated that specific bacterial or fungal GH3 enzymes can degrade amygdalin (Gao and Wakarchuk, 2014; Guo et al., 2015; Chang and Zhang, 2012; Li et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Ten other Bifidobacterium strains encode a GH3 in their genomes with a high sequence similarity to the wkB204 GH3.
claims.source: Ten other Bifidobacterium strains encode a GH3 in their genomes with a high sequence similarity to the wkB204 GH3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BLAST search results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Bifidobacterium strain wkB344 encodes a GH3 (WP_121913979) with high sequence similarity to the wkB204 GH3.
claims.source: Intriguingly, these included a GH3 from wkB344 (WP_121913979), which did not grow in the presence of amygdalin in vitro.
claims.evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis and phylogenetic data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: In the presence of glucose as the sole carbon source, Bifidobacterium strains wkB204 and wkB344, but not wkB338, express the GH3 gene.
claims.source: In the presence of glucose as the sole carbon source, strains wkB204 and wkB344, but not wkB338, express the GH3 gene (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: When cultivated in the presence of amygdalin as the sole carbon source, only Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 shows elevated expression of GH3 transcripts.
claims.source: When cultivated in the presence of amygdalin as the sole carbon source, only wkB204 shows elevated expression of GH3 transcripts (Figure 5B), which correlates with the ability of this strain to degrade amygdalin in vitro.
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The wkB204 GH3 (WP_254476944) is encoded in an operon containing four other genes: a major facilitator superfamily transporter (WP_254476943), a glycoside hydrolase family 30 (WP_254477160), and a beta-galactosidase (WP_254477161).
claims.source: The wkB204 GH3 (WP_254476944), which is overexpressed in amygdalin-grown cultures, is encoded in an operon containing four other genes: a major facilitator superfamily transporter (WP_254476943), a glycoside hydrolase family 30 (WP_254477160), and a beta-galactosidase (WP_254477161) (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The genes in the wkB204 GH3 operon were also overexpressed in the presence of amygdalin, based on proteomics data.
claims.source: These were also overexpressed in the presence of amygdalin, based on proteomics data (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The wkB344 GH3 (WP_121913979) is encoded in an operon with a beta-galactosidase (WP_121914045) as the only other gene in the operon.
claims.source: The wkB344 GH3 (WP_121913979) is also encoded in an operon, but a beta-galactosidase (WP_121914045) is the only other gene in the operon (Figure 5C), as predicted by the operon-mapper webserver (Taboada et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The genome of Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 encodes 10 distinct GH3s.
claims.source: According to the dbCAN meta server for automated CAZyme annotation, the genomes of these three Bifidobacterium strains encode multiple GH3s: wkB204 encodes 10 distinct GH3s, while wkB344 and wkB338 encode 5 distinct GH3s each (Figure 5—source data 1; Yin et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis using the dbCAN meta server.

claims.claim: The genomes of Bifidobacterium strains wkB344 and wkB338 encode 5 distinct GH3s each.
claims.source: According to the dbCAN meta server for automated CAZyme annotation, the genomes of these three Bifidobacterium strains encode multiple GH3s: wkB204 encodes 10 distinct GH3s, while wkB344 and wkB338 encode 5 distinct GH3s each (Figure 5—source data 1; Yin et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis using the dbCAN meta server.

claims.claim: All Bifidobacterium strains wkB204, wkB344, and wkB338 can degrade prunasin.
claims.source: To investigate whether Bifidobacterium strains can also degrade prunasin, we performed an additional in vitro experiment in which Bifidobacterium strains wkB204, wkB344, and wkB338 were grown in 10 mM glucose in SDM in the presence of 0.1 mM prunasin (Figure 6A). Under these conditions, all strains grew in the presence of prunasin (Figure 6B) and degraded it (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by growth and LC-MS data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claims.claim: Bifidobacterium strain wkB344 can degrade 0.1 mM amygdalin.
claims.source: For comparison, we also checked growth in the presence of 0.1 mM amygdalin (Figure 6D) and found that not only wkB204, but also wkB344 degraded amygdalin (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: The lack of growth and degradation observed for Bifidobacterium strain wkB344 at higher amygdalin concentrations is probably due to the much higher concentration of amygdalin provided in previous cultures (10 or 100 mM).
claims.source: The lack of growth and, consequently, of degradation observed before for this strain is probably due to the much higher concentration of amygdalin provided in previous cultures (10 or 100 mM).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that wkB344 can degrade amygdalin at lower concentrations but not at higher concentrations.

claims.claim: Cell lysates of transformed E. coli expressing wkB204-GH3 or wkB344-GH3 degraded amygdalin and produced prunasin.
claims.source: After 5 days of incubation, we observed amygdalin degradation (Figure 7D) followed by prunasin production (Figure 7E) for E. coli cell lysates expressing either wkB204-GH3 or wkB344-GH3, but not for E. coli transformed with an empty plasmid, indicating that both enzymes can degrade amygdalin into prunasin.
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 7D-E.

claims.claim: The Bifidobacterium-related GH3 enzyme can degrade prunasin, but to a lesser extent than amygdalin under the tested conditions.
claims.source: When the cell lysates were incubated in the presence of prunasin, only a small amount of prunasin was degraded (Figure 7F), suggesting that this enzyme, under the tested conditions, still can degrade prunasin, but to a lesser extent.
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: Amygdalin was detected in different compartments of the bee body, including the midgut, the hindgut and the body carcass without the gut of microbiota-deprived, conventionalized, and monocolonized bees.
claims.source: Amygdalin was detected in different compartments of the bee body, including the midgut, the hindgut and the body carcass without the gut of MD, CV, and monocolonized bees (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: In the hindgut samples, amygdalin was detected for microbiota-deprived and wkB344-monocolonized bees but not for conventionalized and wkB204-monocolonized bees.
claims.source: In the hindgut samples, amygdalin was detected for MD and wkB344-monocolonized bees but not for CV and wkB204-monocolonized bees (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Total amygdalin concentration was significantly lower in conventionalized bees and wkB204-monocolonized bees when compared to control bees not treated with amygdalin but spiked with 5 μL of 1 mM amygdalin during the extraction protocol.
claims.source: Total amygdalin concentration was significantly lower in CV bees and wkB204-monocolonized bees when compared to control bees not treated with amygdalin but spiked with 5 μL of 1 mM amygdalin during the extraction protocol (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Prunasin was only detected in the midgut and hindgut of microbiota-deprived bees.
claims.source: Interestingly, prunasin was only detected in the midgut and hindgut of MD bees (Figure 8D–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 8D-E.

claims.claim: The presence of the microbiota contributes to continued amygdalin and prunasin degradation in the bee gut.
claims.source: Therefore, the presence of the microbiota contributes to continued amygdalin and prunasin degradation in the bee gut.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that amygdalin concentration is reduced and prunasin does not accumulate in microbiota-colonized bees.

claims.claim: Honey bees exposed to concentrations of amygdalin, ranging from 0.01 to 1 mM, did not exhibit increased mortality rates or dysbiosis.
claims.source: Honey bees exposed to concentrations of amygdalin, ranging from 0.01 to 1 mM, did not exhibit increased mortality rates or dysbiosis (Figure 9A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by survival data and microbiome analysis shown in Figure 9A-B.

claims.claim: No significant changes were found in gut microbial composition of amygdalin-treated bees when compared to untreated bees.
claims.source: We did not find any significant changes in gut microbial composition (Figure 9C–D) or abundance (Figure 9E) of amygdalin-treated bees when compared to untreated bees, which is consistent with other studies (Tauber et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing data shown in Figure 9C-D.

claims.claim: No significant changes were found in gut microbial abundance of amygdalin-treated bees when compared to untreated bees.
claims.source: We did not find any significant changes in gut microbial composition (Figure 9C–D) or abundance (Figure 9E) of amygdalin-treated bees when compared to untreated bees, which is consistent with other studies (Tauber et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 9E.

claims.claim: Amygdalin did not affect mortality rates of microbiota-deprived bees.
claims.source: Moreover, amygdalin did not affect mortality rates of MD bees (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The concentrations used in the in vivo experiments are below the concentrations detected in almond pollen (~4 mM).
claims.source: The concentrations used in the in vivo experiments are below the concentrations detected in almond pollen (~4 mM), and the lower concentration resembles what has been detected in almond nectar (~0.01 mM) (London-Shafir et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of experimental concentrations to field-relevant concentrations from the literature.

claims.claim: Dietary compounds can be metabolized not only by host enzymes but also by the gut microbiota, potentially resulting in increased or decreased toxicity.
claims.source: Dietary compounds can be metabolized not only by host enzymes but also by the gut microbiota, potentially resulting in increased or decreased toxicity (Koppel et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous review.

claims.claim: The findings for honey bees parallel those for the metabolism of amygdalin in rats, in which the molecule is degraded to produce toxic hydrogen cyanide only in the presence of the gut microbiota.
claims.source: Our findings for honey bees parallel those for the metabolism of amygdalin in rats, in which the molecule is degraded to produce toxic hydrogen cyanide only in the presence of the gut microbiota, but not when microbiota is absent or when injected (Carter et al., 1980).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to findings from a previous study in rats.

claims.claim: Specific members of the bee gut microbiota produce a diverse set of carbohydrate digestive enzymes, including pectin lyases and glycoside hydrolases, that help in food processing.
claims.source: Specific members of the bee gut microbiota produce a diverse set of carbohydrate digestive enzymes, including pectin lyases (PLs) and GHs, that help in food processing (Zheng et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2016; Engel et al., 2012) and detoxification (Berenbaum and Johnson, 2015; Koch et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Gilliamella strains produce pectin lyases and glycoside hydrolases that are involved in the metabolism of pectin and hemicellulose from the pollen cell wall and toxic sugars from nectar or produced during digestion of pectin.
claims.source: For instance, Gilliamella strains produce PLs and GHs that are involved in the metabolism of pectin and hemicellulose from the pollen cell wall and toxic sugars from nectar or produced during digestion of pectin (Zheng et al., 2016; Engel et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Some sugars, such as mannose, arabinose, xylose, and galactose, are indigestible for bees and can cause toxicity if accumulated in the gut.
claims.source: Some of these sugars, such as mannose, arabinose, xylose, and galactose, are indigestible for bees and can cause toxicity if accumulated in the gut (Barker, 1977).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Bombilactobacillus and Lactobacillus strains produce enzymes involved in mannose metabolism which potentially contribute to detoxification.
claims.source: Bombilactobacillus and Lactobacillus strains also produce enzymes involved in mannose metabolism which potentially contribute to this detoxification mechanism (Zheng et al., 2019; Ellegaard et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Genomes of Bifidobacterium strains harbor a wider repertoire of glycoside hydrolases than other core members of the bee gut microbiota, but lack pectin lyase-related genes.
claims.source: Interestingly, genomes of Bifidobacterium strains seem to harbor a wider repertoire of GHs than other core members of the bee gut microbiota, but lack PL-related genes (Zheng et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Bacterial- or fungal-derived GH3s can degrade amygdalin.
claims.source: Other studies have shown that bacterial- or fungal-derived GH3s can degrade amygdalin.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The Gram-positive bacterium Cellulomonas fimi encodes a GH3 with activity against β-1,6-linked glycosides.
claims.source: For example, the Gram-positive bacterium Cellulomonas fimi encodes a GH3 with activity against β-1,6-linked glycosides (Gao and Wakarchuk, 2014), similar to the linkage found in the structure of amygdalin (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Degradation of amygdalin by GH3s isolated from Rhizomucor miehei and Talaromyce leycettanus has been observed.
claims.source: Degradation of amygdalin by GH3s isolated from Rhizomucor miehei (Guo et al., 2015) and Talaromyce leycettanus (Li et al., 2018), or by related extracellular enzymes from Aspergillus niger, has also been observed (Chang and Zhang, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Different species of mammalian gut-associated Bifidobacterium strains can grow in the presence of amygdalin, potentially due to the production of GH1 or GH3 enzymes.
claims.source: Moreover, different species of mammalian gut-associated Bifidobacterium strains can grow in the presence of amygdalin, potentially due to the production of GH1 or GH3 enzymes (Modrackova et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Heterologous expression of wkB204-GH3 or wkB344-GH3 using E. coli led to amygdalin degradation, but to a lesser extent than what was observed for the original host.
claims.source: In our case, heterologous expression of wkB204-GH3 (WP_254476944) or wkB344-GH3 (WP_121913979) using E. coli also led to amygdalin degradation, but to a lesser extent than what was observed for the original host.
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data from heterologous expression experiments (Figure 7).

claims.claim: There may be other carbohydrate digestive enzymes encoded by Bifidobacterium that contribute to amygdalin or prunasin metabolism.
claims.source: Potentially, there are other carbohydrate digestive enzymes encoded by Bifidobacterium that contribute to amygdalin or prunasin metabolism (Figure 4C), or the Bifidobacterium host perform specific posttranslational modifications on this enzyme that are not achieved during heterologous expression in E. coli (Adav et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is speculated based on proteomics data showing multiple upregulated enzymes.

claims.claim: The Bifidobacterium host may perform specific posttranslational modifications on the GH3 enzyme that are not achieved during heterologous expression in E. coli.
claims.source: Potentially, there are other carbohydrate digestive enzymes encoded by Bifidobacterium that contribute to amygdalin or prunasin metabolism (Figure 4C), or the Bifidobacterium host perform specific posttranslational modifications on this enzyme that are not achieved during heterologous expression in E. coli (Adav et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is speculated based on the observation of lower degradation rates in E. coli.

claims.claim: The GH3 enzyme appears to be secreted by Bifidobacterium strain wkB204.
claims.source: Moreover, it seems this GH3 is secreted by Bifidobacterium strain wkB204, but, for cloning purposes, we expressed it in E. coli without a signal sequence for secretion, and, therefore, performed assays with cell lysates, which may not be optimal for characterizing enzyme activity.
claims.evidence: This is supported by biochemical assays showing amygdalin degradation in spent medium (Figure 3B).

claims.claim: Nectar and pollen metabolites can be chemically transformed when passing through the gut, and this may influence their effects on the host and/or the microbiota.
claims.source: As shown in other studies, nectar and pollen metabolites can be chemically transformed when passing through the gut, and this may influence their effects on the host and/or the microbiota (Koch et al., 2019; Vidkjær et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Amygdalin is absorbed systemically by bee cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, we also found amygdalin in bee carcasses with the gut removed, suggesting that amygdalin is absorbed systemically by bee cells. This has been observed in other studies in which amygdalin was found in the bee hemolymph after oral ingestion (Hurst et al., 2014; Vidkjær et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data showing amygdalin in body carcasses (Figure 8B) and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Studies in rats have found higher concentrations of hydrogen cyanide in the blood of microbiota-colonized rats than in microbiota-deprived rats or antibiotic-treated rats after oral ingestion of amygdalin.
claims.source: Studies in rats, for example, have found higher concentrations of hydrogen cyanide in the blood of microbiota-colonized rats than in MD rats (Carter et al., 1980) or antibiotic-treated rats (Newton et al., 1981) after oral ingestion of amygdalin.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Intravenous administration of amygdalin does not lead to hydrogen cyanide formation.
claims.source: However, intravenous administration of amygdalin seems not to lead to hydrogen cyanide formation (Jaswal and Palanivelu, 2018), which could be correlated to the lack of toxicity observed in honey bees after amygdalin injection into the hemolymph (Hurst et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The gut microbiota is a major factor driving amygdalin degradation and hydrogen cyanide release in the guts of animals.
claims.source: These studies suggest that the gut microbiota is a major factor driving amygdalin degradation and hydrogen cyanide release in the guts of animals.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from studies in rats and bees showing microbiota-dependent degradation.

claims.claim: Colonization by the normal microbiota decreases the pH to about 5 in the bee gut.
claims.source: It is important to note that colonization by the normal microbiota decreases the pH to about 5 in the bee gut (Zheng et al., 2017), and low pH can favor the degradation of amygdalin into prunasin, then prunasin into mandelonitrile, which can undergo spontaneous degradation at acidic pH to give benzaldehyde and hydrogen cyanide (Jaswal and Palanivelu, 2018).

results.result: Both honey bee hosts and their gut microbiota contribute to amygdalin metabolism. In microbiota-deprived bees, amygdalin is partially degraded to prunasin which accumulates in the gut, while in microbiota-colonized bees, amygdalin is further degraded and prunasin does not accumulate, suggesting complete degradation to hydrogen cyanide by the microbiota.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C5, C39-C40, C82-C83 are supported by in vivo LC-MS data (Figure 8) showing prunasin accumulation only in microbiota-deprived bees and reduced amygdalin levels in microbiota-colonized bees. The conclusion (C12) that host and microbiota act together is well-supported by converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches.

results.result: Amygdalin degradation by bee gut bacteria is strain-specific, not genus- or species-specific. Specific strains of Bifidobacterium (wkB204), Bombilactobacillus (BI-1.1, BI-2.5), and Gilliamella (wkB112) can degrade amygdalin, with different degradation mechanisms: some strains produce prunasin as an intermediate (wkB204, BI-1.1) while others do not (BI-2.5, wkB112).
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8, C41-C56 are well-supported by in vitro growth assays and LC-MS data (Figures 1-2) showing strain-level variation in amygdalin degradation capacity and mechanism. The data clearly demonstrate that degradation ability varies within genera and that different strains use different pathways (prunasin intermediate vs. direct cleavage).

results.result: Bifidobacterium wkB204 fully degrades amygdalin and overexpresses/secretes several carbohydrate-degrading enzymes when grown with amygdalin, including a glycoside hydrolase family 3 (GH3) enzyme (WP_254476944) detected only in amygdalin-grown cultures.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C57-C63 are supported by growth data (Figure 1), biochemical assays showing degradation in spent medium (Figure 3), SDS-PAGE (Figure 4B), and proteomics analysis (Figure 4C) identifying 107 upregulated proteins including the GH3 enzyme. The convergence of multiple lines of evidence strongly supports these findings.

results.result: A GH3 enzyme from Bifidobacterium wkB204 (WP_254476944) contributes to amygdalin degradation. When expressed in E. coli, cell lysates degraded amygdalin and produced prunasin, though to a lesser extent than the native host. The GH3 gene is highly expressed in wkB204 when grown with amygdalin but not in related strain wkB344.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C63, C65-C68, C77-C78, C100 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 5B), heterologous expression experiments (Figure 7D-E), and genomic analysis (Figure 5). The heterologous expression provides direct evidence for GH3 involvement, though the lower activity in E. coli (C100) suggests additional factors may be required for full activity.

results.result: All three Bifidobacterium strains tested (wkB204, wkB344, wkB338) can degrade prunasin at 0.1 mM concentration. Additionally, wkB344 can degrade 0.1 mM amygdalin, though it cannot degrade higher concentrations (10-100 mM), suggesting concentration-dependent toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76 are supported by growth and LC-MS data (Figure 6). The data clearly show all strains degrade prunasin and that wkB344 can degrade amygdalin at lower concentrations. The inference about concentration-dependent toxicity (C76) is reasonable given the contrasting results at different concentrations.

results.result: The wkB204 GH3 (WP_254476944) is encoded in an operon with four other genes including a transporter, another glycoside hydrolase, and a beta-galactosidase, all overexpressed with amygdalin. The wkB344 GH3 operon contains only a beta-galactosidase. wkB204 encodes 10 distinct GH3s while wkB344 and wkB338 each encode 5.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C73 are supported by genomic analysis (Figure 5C) and proteomics data showing operon gene overexpression. The dbCAN annotation provides the GH3 counts. This genomic context helps explain differential regulation and activity between strains.

results.result: Amygdalin was detected in multiple bee body compartments (midgut, hindgut, body carcass) after oral exposure, indicating systemic absorption. Amygdalin concentration was significantly lower in conventionalized and wkB204-monocolonized bees compared to controls, and was not detected in hindguts of these groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81, C105 are supported by LC-MS data from in vivo experiments (Figure 8B-C). The detection of amygdalin in body carcasses without gut provides direct evidence for systemic absorption. The differential distribution across treatment groups supports microbiota-dependent degradation.

results.result: Honey bees exposed to field-relevant concentrations of amygdalin (0.01-1 mM) did not exhibit increased mortality or changes in gut microbiota composition or abundance. This was true for both microbiota-colonized and microbiota-deprived bees.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87, C112 are supported by survival data (Figure 9A-B, Figure 9—figure supplement 1), 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing (Figure 9C-D), and qPCR (Figure 9E). The lack of adverse effects at field-relevant concentrations is well-documented and consistent with prior studies (C38).

results.result: Amygdalin is a cyanogenic glycoside found in almond nectar (~0.01 mM) and pollen (~4 mM). It is degraded through prunasin and mandelonitrile to produce toxic hydrogen cyanide. Bees can tolerate concentrations up to 219 μM without mortality effects, though higher doses cause malaise symptoms.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C15-C25, C88 are supported by citations to established literature. These provide essential background context for the study. The degradation pathway (C18-C20) is well-established biochemistry, and bee tolerance data (C23-C24) comes from prior studies.

results.result: Bee genomes have lower detoxification gene diversity than other insects but encode some xenobiotic-metabolizing enzymes including cytochrome P450s, glutathione transferases, and glycoside hydrolases. Honey bees secrete a GH from hypopharyngeal glands that may catalyze initial glycoside breakdown in the midgut.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C14, C31-C33 are supported by citations to genomic studies. This provides important context for why bees may rely on microbiota for detoxification (C14), though C14 itself is an inference rather than a directly tested hypothesis in this study.

results.result: Amygdalin toxicity occurs after ingestion but not injection into hemolymph, suggesting gut enzymes convert it to hydrogen cyanide. The dominant bee gut bacterial species produce diverse glycoside hydrolases. Amygdalin itself shows no antibacterial effects and does not significantly affect the bee gut microbiota.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 are supported by citations (C34, C36-C37) and the authors' own data (C38, Figure 9). The inference about gut enzyme involvement (C35) is reasonable given the route-dependent toxicity, though the specific enzymes were not directly identified in the cited study.

results.result: High doses of amygdalin cause acute malaise symptoms and reduced survivorship in bees, while lower doses can also reduce survivorship in lab trials. However, colony-level amygdalin exposure may protect against parasites like Lotmaria passim and reduce viral titers.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C30 are supported by citations to prior studies. This provides important context about the dual nature of amygdalin effects (toxic at high doses, potentially protective at lower doses), though these are not findings of the current study.

results.result: Bacterial and fungal GH3 enzymes from various organisms (Cellulomonas fimi, Rhizomucor miehei, Talaromyces leycettanus, Aspergillus niger, and mammalian gut-associated Bifidobacterium) can degrade amygdalin, as demonstrated in prior studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C64, C96-C99 are supported by citations to prior literature. This provides important comparative context showing that amygdalin-degrading GH3s are found across diverse organisms, supporting the plausibility of the authors' findings in bee gut bacteria.

results.result: Dietary compounds can be metabolized by both host and microbiota, affecting toxicity. Studies in rats show microbiota-dependent amygdalin degradation to hydrogen cyanide, paralleling the bee findings. The microbiota lowers gut pH to ~5, which can favor spontaneous chemical degradation of amygdalin through prunasin to mandelonitrile and hydrogen cyanide.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90, C104, C106-C111 are supported by citations to prior studies. The comparison to rat studies (C90, C106-C108) strengthens the interpretation of the bee data. The pH-dependent degradation mechanism (C109-C111) provides an alternative or complementary explanation to enzymatic degradation.

results.result: Bee gut microbiota members produce diverse carbohydrate-degrading enzymes for food processing and detoxification. Gilliamella produces pectin lyases and glycoside hydrolases for pollen cell wall metabolism and toxic sugar degradation. Bombilactobacillus and Lactobacillus produce mannose metabolism enzymes. Bifidobacterium strains have more glycoside hydrolases but lack pectin lyases.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C95 are supported by citations to prior genomic and functional studies. This provides important context about the broader role of the microbiota in carbohydrate metabolism and detoxification, situating amygdalin degradation within a larger functional framework.

results.result: The lower amygdalin degradation activity in E. coli expressing the GH3 compared to native Bifidobacterium may be due to other contributing enzymes or posttranslational modifications not achieved in E. coli. The GH3 appears to be secreted by wkB204 but was expressed without a signal sequence in E. coli.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 are speculative explanations for the lower activity in heterologous expression. While C103 is supported by data showing degradation in spent medium (Figure 3B), C101-C102 are reasonable hypotheses but lack direct experimental support. Additional experiments would be needed to test these explanations.

results.result: Plant secondary metabolites can improve pollinator health by controlling parasites, and insects including bees use toxic metabolites for therapeutic or prophylactic self-medication. However, effectiveness depends on the specific metabolite, concentration, and target parasite. For example, amygdalin reduces Lotmaria passim but not Crithidia in bees.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C124 are supported by citations to prior studies. This provides important ecological and evolutionary context for understanding why bees might tolerate and even benefit from amygdalin exposure despite its potential toxicity. The examples from other insects (monarchs, fruit flies) illustrate broader patterns of insect self-medication.

results.result: Host and microbiota can modulate plant metabolite activity through glycosylation/deglycosylation. Examples include callunene (prophylactic but not therapeutic due to host inactivation), tiliaside (requires deglycosylation for activity), and unedone (glycosylated/inactivated in midgut, then deglycosylated/reactivated in hindgut). Bee gut bacteria can metabolize flavonoid glycosides and encode diverse glycoside hydrolases.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C133 are supported by citations to recent studies. This provides important comparative context showing that the amygdalin findings fit within a broader pattern of host-microbiota cooperation in metabolizing plant glycosides, with spatial and temporal regulation of activity.

results.result: Strain-level variation in microbiome metabolism could affect parasite establishment, and microbiota perturbation by pesticides or heavy metals could indirectly affect parasites through altered secondary metabolite metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C135 are speculative inferences from the study's findings about strain variation. While C134 is a reasonable inference from the demonstrated strain-specific metabolism, C135 is highly speculative and would require substantial additional research to test. These represent potential future research directions rather than supported conclusions.

results.result: Bee gut microbiota interactions with pathogens are widespread, with the core microbiota protecting against viruses, bacterial infections, and Nosema. Mechanisms may involve host immunity and/or direct microbial interactions. Microbial metabolism of dietary components is one mechanism through which microbiota impact hosts or co-resident microbes.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C141 are supported by citations to prior studies establishing microbiota-pathogen interactions. Claim C142 is the main conclusion of the current study, supported by the experimental data. This situates the amygdalin findings within the broader context of microbiota-mediated protection.
